summary:
Rotation Explorer is a free, multilingual web tool that helps farmers and advisers compare crop rotations for any place on Earth using NASA Earth observations. The user picks a location, sets what matters most (saving water, income, soil health) and gets at least three rotations ranked in plain words, always including the one they grow now.

Scores come from 20 years of NASA POWER weather plus MODIS vegetation greenness, SMAP soil moisture and GPM IMERG rainfall, with ISRIC SoilGrids soil maps. This answers "Adapting Farms with NASA Data" by turning satellite data into a decision a farmer can read, not a yield forecast.

Every result shows a range, its data gaps and why it is or is not trustworthy, labels observed versus modelled data, and tells users to check with a local agronomist. A crop map uses real land-cover data and never invents fields. Hero case: wheat-on-wheat in Punjab, Pakistan. Works on phones, offline, in 10 languages, with no sign-up.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Rotation Explorer compares crop rotations for a field location. The user searches a town, uses GPS or taps the map, then sets three priorities (water saving, income/yield risk, soil building) and whether the land is irrigated. The tool ranks at least three rotations, always including the current one, and explains each result in plain language with its score range, data gaps and risks. Nine ready-made places (Lahore, Islamabad, Rawalpindi, Ludhiana, Dhaka, Nairobi, Londrina, Toowoomba, Ames) use real cached NASA data; any other place on Earth is looked up live.

HOW IT WORKS

Scoring is rule-based and fully visible: six factors (water demand vs. supply, heat and frost exposure, bare-field exposure, soil fit, soil organic carbon effect, extreme-rain risk) are scored for each of 20 years, weighted by the sliders, and summarised as a mean with a low-to-high range. NASA POWER gives the 20-year weather record. MODIS NDVI shows when fields sit bare. SMAP soil moisture and GPM IMERG rainfall adjust the water supply by at most 7.5% each, so recent satellite readings never replace the long record. ISRIC SoilGrids (not NASA) provides soil pH, clay and carbon. A crop map layer uses the USDA Cropland Data Layer (USA) and ESA WorldCover (cropland elsewhere); where crop type is unavailable the app says so instead of inventing it. What-if sliders change rain and temperature, a comparison tool puts two places side by side, and results can be shared by link or printed.

IMPACT

Many farms grow the same crop on the same land year after year while soil carbon and irrigation water decline. The tool lets a farmer or adviser see, for their own location, which rotations suit the climate and soil, how certain that is, and what is missing, then take that to a local agronomist. It is free, needs no sign-up, works on phones and offline, and is available in 10 languages including Urdu, Arabic, Hindi, Bengali and Swahili.

TOOLS

HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript with Leaflet maps (no framework); Python 3.12 with FastAPI, rasterio, h5py, pandas and numpy for an optional backend on Render; GitHub Pages and GitHub Actions for hosting and 12 JavaScript test suites plus 103 Python tests; NASA Harmony and Earthdata services for SMAP and IMERG; Microsoft Planetary Computer for the crop layer.

CREATIVITY AND FACTORS CONSIDERED

Honesty is the design: observed, satellite-estimated, model-based and calculated values are labelled differently; confidence is explained in words; missing data shows as "n/a" or a gap note; farmers never log in and no NASA credential is ever in the browser. Limits are stated: results describe the surrounding area (kilometres), not one field; crop rules are rules of thumb; irrigation, pests and prices are not modelled; the score is a relative comparison, not a yield forecast.

SUPER INTELLIGENCE

AI (Claude by Anthropic) was used for ideation, research on data sources, data analysis, coding and debugging, writing and translation (10 languages), and visual design (layout, logo and icons drawn as code). The product itself contains no AI or machine learning: scoring is transparent rule-based logic. No photos, video or audio were AI-generated; the satellite imagery is real NASA GIBS data. No NASA logos or mission marks are used. The disclosure is in the README and the site footer.
